post.title: LLM Model Quantization: Why, When, and How to Deploy Smaller, Faster Models
post.subtitle: Cut GPU memory and latency by converting FP16 weights to INT8 or INT4 — without retraining from scratch.
post.brief: Quantization converts high-precision model weights and activations (FP16/FP32) into lower-precision formats (INT8 or INT4) so LLMs run with less memory, lower latency, and lower cost. The key is choosing the right quantization method for your accuracy budget, hardware, and traffic pattern.

content.markdown:
## Scenario context

Quantization converts high-precision model weights and activations (FP16/FP32) into lower-precision formats (INT8 or INT4) so LLMs run with less memory, lower latency, and lower cost. The key is choosing the right quantization method for your accuracy budget, hardware, and traffic pattern.

---

If you have ever tried to serve a 7B or 13B model in production, you already know the pain points:

- GPU memory fills up…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Quantization Matters for LLM Deployments**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- If you have ever tried to serve a 7B or 13B model in production, you already know the pain points: - GPU memory fills up fast.
- - Throughput falls when context length grows.
- - Inference bills scale faster than user growth.

**Concepts in play:** quantization-and-llm-inference, deep-learning-foundations, caching, canary-deployments

## Stage 1 — Bits, Scales, and Zero-Points: Quantization in Plain Language

- At a high level, quantization maps floating-point values to a smaller set of discrete numbers.
- Instead of storing weights as 16-bit or 32-bit floats, you store them as 8-bit or 4-bit values plus metadata (such as scale factors) to approximately reconstruct original values during compute.
- Common quantization families Common precision targets 📊 Precision vs Size Trade-off This diagram maps the four common numeric precision formats — FP32, FP16, INT8, and INT4 — as a linear chain from largest to smallest.
- Moving from FP32 to FP16 halves memory; moving to INT8 halves it again; reaching INT4 achieves roughly an 8× reduction relative to FP32.

*Applies **quantization-and-llm-inference** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    FP32[FP32 full size] --> FP16[FP16 half size]
    FP16 --> INT8[INT8 quarter size]
    INT8 --> INT4[INT4 eighth size]
    INT4 --> NOTE[Less size more speed]
```

**Observable outcome:** Moving from FP32 to FP16 halves memory; moving to INT8 halves it again; reaching INT4 achieves roughly an 8× reduction relative to FP32.

## Stage 2 — From FP16 Checkpoint to Production Artifact: The Quantization Process

- A reliable quantization workflow is a pipeline, not a one-click conversion.
- Example: "<1.5% drop on eval score, p95 latency -20%, memory -50%." 2.
- Weights only, or weights + activations.
- PTQ INT8 for low risk, or 4-bit (GPTQ/AWQ/NF4 paths) when memory pressure is high.

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    FM[FP32 Model] --> CD[Calibration Data]
    CD --> QP[Quantization Process]
    QP --> I8[INT8 Model]
    QP --> I4[INT4 Model]
    I8 --> DEP[Deploy]
    I4 --> DEP
```

**Observable outcome:** PTQ INT8 for low risk, or 4-bit (GPTQ/AWQ/NF4 paths) when memory pressure is high.

## Stage 3 — Deep Dive: What Changes Inside the Model

- The internals: weights, activations, and kernels Quantization changes both representation and execution path: - Representation: tensors are stored as lower-bit integers (or low-precision floats) plus scale metadata.
- - Arithmetic path: kernels may run integer matrix multiplies and rescale outputs.
- - Memory traffic: fewer bytes move from VRAM/DRAM, often the real bottleneck for decoder inference.
- For LLMs, this matters because generation is frequently memory-bandwidth-bound rather than pure compute-bound.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** For LLMs, this matters because generation is frequently memory-bandwidth-bound rather than pure compute-bound.

## Stage 4 — Edge Cases That Break Naive Quantization

- Quantization fails most often when teams skip workload realism.
- One practical pattern is selective precision: keep the most sensitive modules in higher precision and quantize the rest.

*Applies **canary-deployments** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** One practical pattern is selective precision: keep the most sensitive modules in higher precision and quantize the rest.

## Stage 5 — Visualizing an End-to-End LLM Quantization Flow

- This loop is the operational reality: quantization is iterative, not linear.

*Applies **quantization-and-llm-inference** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Baseline FP16 or FP32 Model] --> B[Define Quality and Latency Targets]
    B --> C[Select Method: PTQ or QAT]
    C --> D[Prepare Calibration and Eval Datasets]
    D --> E[Run Quantization: INT8 or INT4]
    E --> F[Benchmark Memory, Throughput, and p95 Latency]
    F --> G{Quality within budget?}
    G -- No --> H[Adjust Granularity or Precision]
    H --> E
    G -- Yes --> I[Canary Deploy with Fallback]
    I --> J[Full Rollout + Monitoring]
```

**Observable outcome:** This loop is the operational reality: quantization is iterative, not linear.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Applications: Quantization Patterns

- Case study 1: API-hosted assistant - Input: mixed user prompts, medium context, strict latency target.
- - Process: start with INT8 PTQ for all linear layers, keep output head in FP16.
- - Output: lower p95 latency and lower GPU memory, with minimal answer-quality drift.
- Case study 2: edge or on-prem deployment - Input: constrained hardware, low concurrency, strict memory limits.

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Case study 2: edge or on-prem deployment - Input: constrained hardware, low concurrency, strict memory limits.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- - Start with INT8 PTQ unless you have a strong reason to jump directly to 4-bit.
- - Calibration quality matters as much as quantization algorithm choice.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: When to Use INT8, INT4, or Keep Higher Precision

If your model already meets memory and latency targets comfortably, quantization may not be worth the added operational complexity.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Accuracy and Cost

- **Detection:** Intermediate deployments should evaluate at least these trade-offs: - Performance vs cost: lower precision can reduce required GPU count.
